comparator.name: Health Sciences, Policy & Management of Healthcare
comparator.sourceNotes: Fresh 1 November 2026 inspection confirms the current adopted framework and its separately announced 2027–2028 redesign. Verified current 2026–2027 regulatory framework from the actual official 32-page OER (effective 1 September 2026). Articles 3.4–3.6, pages 12–16: eight 15-EC blocks in years 1–2, 25-EC free choice, 15-EC Choices and Dilemmas and 20-EC graduation = 180 unique EC; K/AVV/integration submodules are children and not additional credits. PPO is pass/fail without separate EC in this framework. Article 4.1 and 8.1 require positive first-year BSA for later-year blocks; normally 60 EC plus PPO with article 3.5 first-year compensation (one 5.0–5.4 compensated by another module at least 6.0). No between-module compensation in years 2–3. Graduation entry requires all B1/B2 components and a timely secured placement; the three GW310/GW311/GW312 codes represent alternative start trajectories for one 20-EC project, not cumulative projects. Free choice permits approved minors/electives/exchange/international placement under article 3.6; outside LDE universities needs examination-board permission requested at least eight weeks in advance; exchange needs board-approved non-overlapping on-campus formally assessed courses, at least half B2 level, minimum 25 EC; international placements of 10/15 EC need coordinator approval. Required mentoring/coaching/intervision and stated participation requirements are non-credit obligations. Honours is extracurricular. Appendix 1, page 31, explicitly starts the redesigned curriculum in 2027–2028: free choice changes from 25 to 30 EC, graduation from 20 to 30 EC and Block 9 from 15 to zero. The public programme page’s 30 EC therefore is not imported into the retained 2026–2027 framework. This is a year-specific regulatory snapshot, not a guarantee that a new entrant will retain unchanged rules throughout three future years.
components: 25 EC chosen from permitted minors/electives, exchange or international placement under the 2026–2027 OER; relevant admission and approval conditions apply.
Placement-based independent research comprising responsibility for the problem statement, design, fieldwork and report.

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory

core: Healthcare systems, policy, governance, law and public decision-making
Health economics, affordability, insurance, markets and allocation
Healthcare organisations, management, quality and stakeholder coordination
Public health, epidemiology, prevention and social-medical perspectives on health and illness
Health behaviour, medical sociology, inequality, culture and stigma
Qualitative and quantitative healthcare research, evidence assessment and academic communication
Ethical dilemmas and interdisciplinary choices in healthcare
Independent applied health research in an organisational setting
adjacent: Ageing, lifecourse needs and future care
Youth care, mental healthcare and welfare
questions: How should government, markets and insurance organise accessible and affordable healthcare?
How do governments, insurers, organisations, professionals and patients interact in healthcare?
How can complex health problems be analysed and addressed across social, behavioural, legal, economic and organisational perspectives?

trace: provides mandatory first-year source evaluation, communication, reflection and civic formation; it is not an organisational research placement
provides complementary financial-statement and accounting analysis; healthcare budgets or hospital logistics are not required applications
provides complementary microeconomic/macroeconomic concepts for analysing markets and allocation, without specialised health-insurance teaching
provides complementary consumer/producer theory, uncertainty, imperfect competition, factor markets, efficiency and government intervention; medical insurance is not a required case

Studies public goods, market failure, taxation, spending and redistribution, with explicit health, education, welfare and social-insurance applications. Models, data, research appraisal and a paper/proposal provide allocation tools; this is not Dutch insurance-law training.
provides complementary causal/predictive empirical methods using OLS, GLS, instruments, statistical tests and an empirical paper; no health-data application is guaranteed
provides complementary general research design and descriptive/inferential statistics, including group research; it is not specialist health-services methodology
provides complementary organisational behaviour, motivation, leadership, power, groups, structure and culture; it does not require hospital management cases
provides complementary legal-system, rights and justice foundations; it is not Dutch healthcare-system or patient-law training
provides complementary legal, historical and philosophical human-rights analysis, without a health-law or patient-rights specialisation
provides complementary comparative constitutional/administrative law, government powers and rights; healthcare regulation is not required content
provides complementary normative theories and practical ethical argument; its actual cases do not establish a medical-ethics curriculum
provides complementary empirical comparison of political institutions, democracy and state-society relations; it does not teach the healthcare policy cycle
provides complementary social theory, social institutions and race/gender/class analysis; medical sociology is not required content
provides complementary qualitative research design, collection, interpretation, reflexivity and dissemination; no healthcare fieldwork requirement is inferred
provides complementary social theory of modernity, imperialism and colonial responses; it is not a health-institution course
provides complementary civil-society theory, solidarity and NGO/community research; healthcare organisations are not a required setting
directly studies epidemiology, disease risk and patterns, prevention, population health and critical assessment of public-health evidence
Develops molecular, cellular and biochemical foundations, genetics and scientific evidence appraisal for disease science; it does not supply complete organ physiology or health policy.
provides the psychological/neuroscientific foundation and formal gateway for selected psychology courses; it is not clinical practice training
provides complementary social-psychological theories and evidence about the influence of others on thoughts, feelings and behaviour
provides multivariate statistics, regression, factor analysis, (co)variance analysis and non-parametric methods for empirical research; it is not health-economics evaluation
directly studies mental health and disorders across the lifespan through biological, psychological, social and cultural perspectives; no youth-service policy or care delivery is inferred
directly studies biopsychosocial determinants of health and illness, health behaviour, chronic illness experience and psychological expertise in medical settings

Develops psychological assessment, treatment theories, ethics, test quality and introductory administration, scoring and interpretation skills. A case report and self-monitoring develop clinical skills academically, without supervised-care qualification.

Teaches systematic review, study selection, bias appraisal, effect sizes and fixed/random-effects meta-analysis in R, including heterogeneity, moderators and publication bias. A group meta-analysis and poster support evidence synthesis; this is not an independent healthcare placement.

Studies development from prenatal life through old age and death, biological and environmental influences and case-based assessment/intervention perspectives. A life-story interview with an adult over 50 provides actual developmental inquiry; elder-care organisation is not its subject.

Examines youth radicalisation and educational prevention, risk and protective factors, belonging, inclusive school climates, social-emotional learning and civic agency. Students translate primary research into teacher-training materials and a youth toolkit, then revise using recipient feedback. This is actual youth/prevention communication work, without clinical-trial or youth-service-management equivalence.

Examines fairness, privacy, responsibility, trust and AI ethics alongside psychological perspectives including clinical care, development and social or organisational interaction. Literature synthesis, an analytical psychology project and a podcast provide ethical inquiry; a child/therapy project or complete health-technology implementation is not prescribed.
directly studies physiology and mechanisms of disease across six organ systems; this supplies scientific understanding of illness rather than clinical service delivery

Uses customer/problem discovery, design thinking, solution prototyping, value propositions and business models in a startup plan, pitch and simulation. These innovation methods complement the health-needs foundation; a health project is not guaranteed.

Develops customer needs, specifications, concept selection, production plans and prototypes where feasible, with cost, scaling, repairability and circularity considerations. These are product innovation methods; a medical product or healthcare service is not prescribed.

Studies consumer psychology, customer insights, marketing and responsible brand development. Projects design a brand, investigate strategy/consumer behaviour and map customer journeys. These user/adoption methods complement health-needs inquiry; patient projects are not prescribed.

Develops strategic planning, digital value opportunities, business models and responsible digital transformation. Provides organisational innovation and technology foresight tools; a healthcare implementation project is not guaranteed.

Plans and carries out customer research, analyses findings and communicates business implications. This evidence gathering complements patient/population inquiry; the description does not establish healthcare fieldwork.

candidates.label: Healthcare markets, insurance and organisational governance

selection.assessment: Three programmes pass the target-level challenge. The closest addresses population health, patient experience and collective allocation/institutional questions. The lifecourse direction sustains developmental and mental-health inquiry. Current entrepreneurship, prototyping, customer research and strategy content supports a distinct innovation direction with substantial health-needs study. Healthcare business projects, placement or specialist innovation training are not assumed. A separate insurance/markets direction converges on the closest after retaining the health anchor and allocation/organisation tools. Three is not a quota: each retained option has an evidenced organising question, material curricular consequences and passed mechanical checks.

alternatives.label: Population health, institutions & society
alternatives.labelReason: Actual health and population study anchors the programme; institutional and organisational analysis is complementary. The label avoids claiming a specialist healthcare-policy or healthcare-management degree.
alternatives.concept: A population-health programme combines epidemiology, medical and health psychology, lifespan development and disease mechanisms with statistics, qualitative research and research synthesis. Economics, accounting, organisational psychology, public institutions, rights and ethics provide complementary tools for understanding collective choices and organisations. AI Ethics examines privacy, responsibility and psychological applications including clinical care. The programme sustains study of health and illness; its general legal, economic and management courses do not become Dutch health-system, health-insurance or patient-law training.
progression: Current offerings, earlier formal prerequisites, four courses per semester and first-year PPD pass. Research Methods and Statistics precede advanced research synthesis; the innovation schedule places the business gateway before dependent strategy/research and customer research before the late product-design project. Advisory progression was considered separately from formal requirements.

alternatives.label: Lifecourse health & society
alternatives.labelReason: The actual composition supports health needs, psychological development and society across the lifecourse. It does not imply delivery of mental healthcare or professional qualification.
alternatives.concept: This health-and-society programme centres epidemiology, health psychology, psychopathology, lifespan development, youth resilience, psychological assessment and research synthesis. Sociology, qualitative methods, public economics, organisations, rights and ethics support inquiry into health needs, social conditions and collective choices. AI Ethics adds inquiry into privacy, responsibility and psychological applications including clinical care. Introductory assessment practice and therapeutic approaches develop clinical skills academically; they do not confer professional qualification or reproduce the external degree’s integrated youth-service and healthcare-policy practice.
alternatives.distinctness: The programmes share 18 courses, with 6 different courses (45 EC) in each. The closest adds biological/disease science, accounting, microeconomics and econometrics; the related programme adds social psychology and psychopathology, youth resilience, assessment practice and therapeutic approaches, modern sociology and constitutional comparison. Their organising questions differ between population/institutional analysis and development, mental health and social conditions across the lifecourse.
progression: Current offerings, earlier formal prerequisites, four courses per semester and first-year PPD pass. Research Methods and Statistics precede advanced research synthesis; the innovation schedule places the business gateway before dependent strategy/research and customer research before the late product-design project. Advisory progression was considered separately from formal requirements.

alternatives.label: Health needs, innovation & organisations
alternatives.labelReason: A substantial epidemiology, health-psychology, lifespan and evidence base supports inquiry into health needs. Five innovation, customer and strategy courses replace biological/disease science, econometrics, the legal gateway and civil-society study from the closest programme. Prototyping, customer research, brand/customer-journey work and strategic planning implement the distinct organisational innovation direction.
alternatives.concept: A health-needs and innovation programme combines epidemiology, patient experience, lifespan development and research synthesis with entrepreneurship, product development, customer research, marketing and digital strategy. Public economics, accounting, organisational psychology, rights and ethics support decisions about resources, users and implementation. Health courses investigate population needs and patient experience; business courses develop prototypes where feasible, customer insights and strategic plans. Their projects are not guaranteed to use healthcare settings or products. This offers related study of health needs and organisational innovation, rather than specialist health-service design, Dutch health-system training or a required healthcare placement.
alternatives.distinctness: Five courses (37.5 EC) differ from the closest and eight (60 EC) from the lifecourse option. Startup and product development, customer insights, market research and digital strategy shift inquiry toward innovation development and adoption. The retained health-needs core makes this a related response to healthcare innovation; the business projects themselves are not guaranteed healthcare applications.
progression: Current offerings, earlier formal prerequisites, four courses per semester and first-year PPD pass. Research Methods and Statistics precede advanced research synthesis; the innovation schedule places the business gateway before dependent strategy/research and customer research before the late product-design project. Advisory progression was considered separately from formal requirements.

blocks: Public health, health, illness & care across the lifespan

Both directly examine how biological, psychological and social factors shape health, illness and patient experience. Erasmus also integrates legal patient status and questions about health knowledge; UCR concentrates on health psychology.
Both study change across the lifecourse and older age. UCR supplies developmental psychology; Erasmus integrates care needs, ageing and social/organisational/government responses.
Health psychology and youth resilience inform service-user needs, but do not directly deliver the block’s youth-service policy, legal responsibilities, waiting lists and stakeholder project.
Healthcare systems, law, public institutions & ethics

Both examine ethical questions about data and technology in care. UCR addresses privacy, responsibility and psychological applications including clinical care; Erasmus integrates a broader set of healthcare dilemmas.
General law and political science do not deliver the Dutch healthcare system’s institutions, financing arrangements and healthcare-specific legal framework.

Both use economic analysis of consumer/provider behaviour, market structures and intervention. UCR teaches general microeconomics; Erasmus specifically studies insurer/provider and insurance markets and their legal rules.

Both directly examine organisational structures, culture, leadership, groups and coordination. UCR supplies general organisational behaviour, while Erasmus integrates healthcare organisations, financial/logistical data and observation.

Both develop an innovation from user needs through a project and its practical or economic development. UCR develops consumer products and prototypes where feasible; Erasmus requires a healthcare innovation, business case and implementation plan. The UCR project is not guaranteed to address healthcare.
Research methods, evidence, communication & professional practice
No scheduled course directly teaches the integrated measurement, improvement, professional regulation and quality governance of healthcare.

The current OER establishes 25 EC of approved minor/elective, exchange or international-placement choice. This has no fixed subject to align; UCR scheduled courses are not presented as a guaranteed approved choice package.

The compulsory 20-EC placement-based independent research/fieldwork project is not delivered by the scheduled research-synthesis seminar. Optional independent research is displayed separately outside the UCR 180 EC; it does not fulfil the required external placement.

notes.text: The UCR programmes combine population health, health psychology and related biological or developmental study with research methods and complementary social, economic, organisational and legal tools. They do not reproduce the Dutch healthcare system, specialist health law, healthcare quality/insurance framework or the required organisation-based research placement.

audience.programmeDescription: Health Sciences, Policy & Management of Healthcare at Erasmus studies health services through economics, law, social-medical science, public policy, organisations and ethics. Its Dutch-taught, full-time BSc combines thematic study with research and practical projects.
audience.comparisonExplanation: Three UCR programmes combine actual health-focused inquiry with different supporting fields. The closest emphasises population health, institutions and allocation; the second emphasises development, mental health and social conditions; the third adds prototyping, customer research and strategic planning to a health-needs foundation. These are related approaches to health and collective or organisational choices. They do not reproduce specialist Dutch health-system, insurance, health-law or quality training, or the required healthcare research placement. Business projects in the innovation option are not guaranteed to use healthcare settings. Shared rows show partial relationships; blank cells preserve other content and gaps.
